Every data scientist writes code that does not work, and professional developers spend between twenty and forty percent of their working time finding out why. Debugging is a skill distinct from programming, which means that strong programmers are not automatically strong debuggers and that the skill has to be practiced on its own terms. In this discussion section, you will:

- Read a Python traceback and locate the line that caused the error
- Apply a systematic debugging protocol instead of changing code at random
- Recognize silent bugs, which produce wrong results without raising any error
- Keep a debugging log, so that a hard-won fix is not lost by next week
- Write assertions that make bugs announce themselves early
- Write a minimal reproducible example to ask for help effectively

## The two-stage protocol

:::{.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
## Keep this open for the whole section

Debugging has two stages, and they ask different questions. Work through them in order, because a program that does not run cannot be checked for correctness.

**Stage 1. Does the code run?** If not, you have a **loud bug**, and the traceback is telling you where to look.

**Stage 2. Is the answer right?** If the code runs but the result is wrong, you have a **silent bug**, and nothing will tell you except your own expectations.

Inside either stage, the loop is the same six steps.

1. **Read the error**, or state the mismatch. Note the error *type*, the *message*, and the last line of the traceback that points at **your** code.
2. **Look at the data.** Check `.shape`, `.dtypes`, `.columns`, and `.head()`. Most bugs are a mismatch between the data you have and the data you assumed.
3. **Isolate.** Reduce the failing code to the smallest piece that still breaks.
4. **Form a hypothesis and test it.** State what you think is wrong in one sentence, then write code that confirms or rejects it.
5. **Fix, then verify.** Re-run from the top and confirm the fix did not break something downstream.
6. **Add a guard**, so the bug announces itself if it ever returns.

If a change does not fix the problem, **undo it before trying the next thing.** Novice programmers routinely introduce new bugs while hunting an old one, and a pile of half-reverted edits is how a one-bug problem becomes a three-bug problem.
:::

## About the data

:::{.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
For this section you will use a small **constructed** dataset of stream monitoring measurements from three sites, with 18 rows and six columns.

| Column | Meaning |
| ------ | ------- |
| `site_id` | Monitoring station identifier |
| `date` | Date of the measurement |
| `water_temp_c` | Water temperature, degrees Celsius |
| `discharge_cfs` | Stream discharge, cubic feet per second |
| `nitrate_mg_l` | Nitrate concentration, mg/L |
| `qc_flag` | Quality control flag assigned by the monitoring program |

Unlike the other discussion sections, this data is not from an archive. It is constructed, and it is deliberately small enough to read in full, so that you can always check whether your code produced the right answer by looking at the raw values.

Every problem in it, however, is one you will meet in real environmental data:

- **Sentinel values for missing data.** Many agencies encode "no measurement" as `-999` or `-9999` rather than leaving the field empty. NOAA and USGS products do this routinely.
- **Thousands separators.** Data exported from a spreadsheet often stores `1,240` as text rather than as the number 1240.
- **Detection limits.** Laboratories report concentrations below the instrument's detection limit as `<0.05` rather than as a number, so the whole column arrives as text.
- **Inconsistent identifiers.** Station codes entered by hand pick up trailing spaces and inconsistent capitalization.
:::

## 2. A worked example from start to finish

Your first task is to convert stream discharge from cubic feet per second to cubic metres per second, which means multiplying by 0.0283168. The following cell attempts it and fails.

```python
stream['discharge_cfs'] * 0.0283168
```

Rather than asking you to fix this, **this exercise walks through all six steps so you can see what the protocol looks like in practice.** Read it, run each cell yourself, and confirm you get the same output. The next exercises hand the work back to you a piece at a time.

**Step 1, read the error.** Running the cell gives:

```default
TypeError: can't multiply sequence by non-int of type 'float'
```

The type is `TypeError`, so an operation met a kind of data it cannot work with. The word `sequence` is the clue, because Python calls strings and lists sequences, and multiplying a sequence by an integer repeats it. Python is not refusing to do arithmetic, it is trying to repeat something and finding 0.0283168 is not a whole number of repetitions.

**Step 2, look at the data.**

```python
stream.dtypes
```

`discharge_cfs` is `object`, which is how pandas labels a column of text. A column of measurements has arrived as text.

**Step 3, isolate.** Reduce to the smallest failing piece, which here is a single value.

```python
stream['discharge_cfs'].iloc[0] * 0.0283168   # same TypeError, one value
stream['discharge_cfs'].iloc[0]              # '1,240'
```

**Step 4, form a hypothesis and test it.** The hypothesis is that the thousands separator makes every value text. Test it by looking at the distinct values.

```python
stream['discharge_cfs'].unique()
```

Every value carries a comma, which confirms the hypothesis.

**Step 5, fix and verify.** Remove the separator, convert, then check the result against something you know.

```python
discharge_cms = (stream['discharge_cfs']
                    .str.replace(',', '', regex=False)
                    .astype(float)) * 0.0283168

discharge_cms.head(3)
```

This gives 35.11, 33.41 and 58.05 m³/s. Verify rather than assume, because 1,240 cfs is a little over a thousand and a cubic metre is about 35 cubic feet, so an answer near 35 m³/s is the right order of magnitude. Had the answer come back near 35,000 the conversion would have gone the wrong way.

**Step 6, add a guard.**

```python
assert pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(discharge_cms), 'Discharge failed to convert to numeric'
```

**The log.** Finally, record what happened, because in ten weeks you will meet this bug again and will not remember the fix. Copy this table into a markdown cell and keep adding rows to it as you work through the rest of the section.

| What I expected | What happened | My hypothesis | What I changed | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Discharge in m³/s, around 35 | `TypeError: can't multiply sequence by non-int` | `discharge_cfs` is text because of thousands separators | `.str.replace(',', '')` then `.astype(float)` | Works, 35.11 m³/s, guard added |

**commit, pull, and push changes**
</p>


**Step 1, the error** is `ValueError: could not convert string to float: '<0.05'`.

Notice that this error names the exact value it choked on, which is the fastest route to a fix that any error message gives you. Complete steps 2 through 6.

Step 5 is not purely a coding decision here. The values reported as `<0.05` are measurements that fell below the laboratory's detection limit, so the true concentration lies somewhere between zero and 0.05 mg/L. Discuss with your team what those values should become. There is no single correct answer, and the common conventions include substituting the detection limit itself, substituting half of it, or treating the values as missing. Choose one, implement it, and **write a comment stating what you did and why.**

:::{.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
This part is not really about debugging, and that is deliberate. Code that raises no error can still encode a scientific decision that a reader needs to know about. A pipeline earns trust when its judgment calls are visible, not merely when it runs cleanly.

```python
# Flag censored values before overwriting them, so the substitution stays visible
stream['nitrate_below_detection'] = stream['nitrate_mg_l'].str.startswith('<')
stream['nitrate_mg_l'] = (stream['nitrate_mg_l']
```

No steps are given. For each cell below, **predict what will happen before you run it**, then work the full protocol and add a row to your log.

```python
# Cell A
stream['temperature'].mean()
```

```python
# Cell B
warm = stream[stream['qc_flag'] == 'good']
warm['water_temp_c'] = warm['water_temp_c'] + 1
```

Cell B is the subtle one. It does not raise an error, it raises a *warning*, and then it does not do what it appears to do. Check whether `warm` actually changed.

<!--
Cell A -> KeyError: 'temperature'. The column is water_temp_c. A KeyError on a data
frame almost always means the label does not exist, so check df.columns for spelling
and stray whitespace. Fix: stream['water_temp_c'].mean()

Cell B -> SettingWithCopyWarning, and the assignment is silently LOST. stream[...]
returns a slice that may be a copy, so the write may land on a temporary object that
is then discarded. Verified: the suspect rows are unchanged afterwards.
Fix, operate on an explicit copy when you want an independent frame:
```python
warm = stream[stream['qc_flag'] == 'good'].copy()
warm['water_temp_c'] = warm['water_temp_c'] + 1
```
Or write back into the original with a single .loc, when that is what you meant:
```python
stream.loc[stream['qc_flag'] == 'good', 'water_temp_c'] += 1
```
The teaching point: a warning is not noise. This one tells you your code did nothing.
-->

d. Complete this table in a markdown cell, using what the four errors you have now met taught you.

| Error type | What it usually means in `pandas` |
| ---------- | --------------------------------- |
| `KeyError` | |
| `AttributeError` | |
| `TypeError` | |
| `ValueError` | |
| `SettingWithCopyWarning` | |

<!--
| KeyError | A column or index label does not exist. Check df.columns for spelling and whitespace. |
| AttributeError | A method was called on the wrong kind of object, e.g. a string method directly on a Series instead of through .str |
| TypeError | An operation met a dtype that does not support it, usually arithmetic on an object (text) column. |
| ValueError | The type is right but a specific value is not acceptable, e.g. a non-numeric string inside astype(float). The message names the value. |
| SettingWithCopyWarning | An assignment may have landed on a copy rather than the original, so it may have done nothing. Use .copy() or a single .loc. |
-->

:::{.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
## Reading a traceback

A traceback reads **bottom to top**. The last line gives the error type and message, which is the single most informative thing on the screen. Above it, Python lists the chain of calls that led there, starting from your cell and descending into library code. The useful line is usually the *lowest* one that names a file you wrote, because everything below it is `pandas` internals and is rarely where your bug lives.

When several errors appear at once, read the **first** one. Later errors are often consequences of the first.
:::

## 5. Bugs that do not raise errors

Everything so far has been stage 1, where Python told you something was wrong. Stage 2 is harder, because the code runs, returns a plausible-looking number, and nothing warns you. Catching these depends entirely on the expectations you recorded in exercise 1c.

a. Run the following cell and compare the result against your expectation from 1c-iii.

```python
stream['water_temp_c'].mean()
```

i. The cell runs without error. Is the answer right, and how do you know?
ii. Explain in one sentence why the result is what it is.
iii. Fix it. Several approaches work, and the best one handles the problem at the moment the data is read, so that no later calculation can ever touch the sentinel.

c. Now a bug that produces no number at all, and still says nothing. You want to attach each site's mean temperature back onto every row.

```python
site_means = stream.groupby('site_id')['water_temp_c'].mean()
stream['site_mean'] = site_means
stream[['site_id', 'water_temp_c', 'site_mean']].head()
```

i. Look at the `site_mean` column. What happened?
ii. Print `site_means` on its own and compare its index to `stream`'s index. Form a hypothesis about why the assignment produced what it did.
iii. Fix it.

:::{.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
## The rule this bug teaches

When you assign a `Series` into a column, pandas aligns the two by **index label**, not by position. Here `site_means` is indexed by `site_id` while `stream` is indexed 0 to 17, so no label matches anything and every row receives `NaN`. Index alignment is usually a convenience, and it is the most common source of pandas results that look right at a glance while being wrong.
:::

<!--
i. Every value in site_mean is NaN. No error, no warning.
ii. site_means has index ['SB-01', 'SB-02', 'SB-03'] while stream has a RangeIndex
    0-17. Assignment aligns on label, finds no overlap, and fills NaN everywhere.
iii. Two correct fixes, which give identical results:
```python
# Map each row's site_id through the lookup
stream['site_mean'] = stream['site_id'].map(site_means)

# Or let groupby broadcast the result back to the original shape
stream['site_mean'] = stream.groupby('site_id')['water_temp_c'].transform('mean')
```
Both give 16.2 for every SB-01 row. Verified identical with .equals().
-->

## 6. Make bugs announce themselves

Step 6 of the protocol is to add a guard. An `assert` statement checks a condition and raises an `AssertionError` with your message when the condition is false, which converts a silent bug into a loud one.

```python
assert condition, 'message explaining what went wrong'
```

a. Write an assertion for each of the following, and confirm each passes on your cleaned data.

i. `stream` has exactly 3 unique sites.
ii. Every water temperature is between -5 and 40 degrees Celsius, ignoring missing values.
iii. `water_temp_c`, `discharge_cfs` and `nitrate_mg_l` are all numeric.

<!--

```python
temps = stream['water_temp_c'].dropna()
assert temps.between(-5, 40).all(), f"Temperature out of range: min {temps.min()}, max {temps.max()}"

for col in ['water_temp_c', 'discharge_cfs', 'nitrate_mg_l']:
    assert pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(stream[col]), f"{col} is {stream[col].dtype}, expected numeric"
```
-->

b. Confirm your guards actually work. Re-load the raw data into a new variable without any cleaning, run your three assertions against it, and check that **each one fails**.

:::{.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
A check you have never seen fail is not a check. An assertion that passes on broken data is testing the wrong thing, and it will hand you false confidence at the exact moment you need real confidence. Every guard you write deserves one run against data you know is bad.
:::

An assertion can be switched off when Python runs with the `-O` flag, so assertions suit checks on things that should never happen inside your own pipeline rather than validation of input a stranger might supply. Discuss with your team which of your three guards you would keep in a script you hand to a colleague, and which you would rewrite to raise a `ValueError` instead.

## 7. Asking for help

When the protocol does not get you there, you ask someone, and how you ask determines whether they can help. A **minimal reproducible example** is the smallest piece of self-contained code that another person can run to see your problem, and it is built from the smallest data that still shows the problem, the shortest code that triggers it, the full error message, and a sentence saying what you expected instead.

a. Choose one bug from this section. In a markdown cell, write a minimal reproducible example of it as though you were posting it for help.

b. Discuss with your team why a three-row example gets a better answer than attaching the full dataset and a sixty-line notebook.

| SB-02   | 15.50        | 3148.33       |
| SB-03   | 13.98        | 618.33        |

Reporting sentences: Mean water temperature ranged from 13.98 degrees C at SB-03 to
16.20 degrees C at SB-01, while mean discharge differed far more across sites, from
618.3 cubic feet per second at SB-03 to 3148.3 at SB-02. Three of the 18 temperature
measurements were recorded as the -999 sentinel and were excluded as missing, and four
nitrate measurements, all at SB-03, fell below the laboratory detection limit.

<p style="text-align: center;">
**commit, pull, and push changes**
</p>

## Takeaways

:::{.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
- A traceback is information, not a punishment. Read the bottom line first, and the first error first.
- Most bugs are a mismatch between the data you have and the data you assumed, so inspect `.dtypes` and `.shape` before changing any code.
- An error that stops your code is a good day, because the bug that returns a plausible wrong number is the one that reaches a published figure.
- You can only catch a silent bug if you know roughly what answer to expect, which makes domain knowledge part of your debugging toolkit.
- Guard every assumption you rely on, and confirm the guard fails on data you know is bad.
- Keep the log. The bug you solve today is one you will meet again, and the fix is cheap to record and expensive to rediscover.
:::
